summary.text: A 67-year-old man with a history of smoking and intermittent alcohol use and intermittent paracetamol use for headache presented to the emergency department with a 15-day history of progressive fatigue, shortness of breath and respiratory insufficiency. On admission he was in poor general condition with severe shortness of breath; he was orthopneic, with blood pressure 80/65 mmHg, pulse 128/minute, a 2/6 systolic murmur in the tricuspid area and 1+ edema of both feet.

The ECG showed an incomplete right bundle branch block, the chest x-ray a dilated pulmonary artery and laboratory tests elevated transaminases; in the light of these data acute toxic hepatitis was the initial diagnosis. CT pulmonary angiography showed no thrombus in the major arteries but a filling defect from the right ventricle to the pulmonary artery, and echocardiography a 6 cm x 5 cm right ventricular mass extending to the pulmonary artery with pulmonary valve invasion and decreased right ventricular function.

He was referred to cardiovascular surgery and operated on as an emergency. The mass proved to be a tumor invading the anterior wall of the right ventricle, interventricular septum and right ventricular outflow tract; it was removed, the resulting ventricular septal defect was closed with a patch and the tricuspid valve was replaced. Pathology showed a poorly differentiated metastatic adenocarcinoma with partial neuroendocrine differentiation.

His postoperative hemodynamic condition did not improve despite inotropic support, and he developed cardiopulmonary arrest on postoperative day 3 and died despite resuscitation attempts. The tumor origin could not be confirmed because the family did not give permission for an autopsy.
